PayPal Agentic Guardrail lets an AI agent take PayPal payments, without ever holding the credential or choosing the payee. Amounts stay inside operator limits.

Our baseline gives the agent a credential and a general HTTP tool. The secret sits in the model context, and hostile product descriptions or invoices can redirect its calls. We test a payment broker that keeps those choices under operator control.

So don't try to make the model trustworthy. Take the choice away from it. The operator binds the payee, the currency and the destination. The agent gets an operation name, and values inside declared ranges. There is no field for a payee, and no field for a URL.
This is the operator's policy. Bound fields are fixed by you. Agent fields are the model's only freedom. Limits apply per call, per day and per hour.

Here it runs. The agent charges and captures. A product note tells it to pay someone else: there is no such parameter. An inflated amount is above the range. A repeat is suppressed, by a key the broker derives within the same fixed one-minute bucket. No operation reveals a secret. A four hundred euro payout waits for a human.
The operator console shows what the agent may do, and what is waiting for a person.
A hash-chained ledger records decisions and refusals. It detects edits against trusted history, not a privileged rewrite of every file.

Now a real model. Qwen reads a hostile product note. Given the credential and an HTTP tool, it pays the attacker's merchant. Through the broker, it creates the right order, because the payee is not its to choose.

We ran thirty tasks, twenty of them attacks, on three real models: five hundred and forty preregistered runs. Without a defence, between seven and twenty six of forty attacks got through, depending on the model. Written security rules did well on two models, and one still let seven through. Through the guardrail: zero, on all three, with fifty nine of sixty benign tasks done.
A scripted agent that obeys everything gives the worst case: one hundred of one hundred attacks blocked, and zero incidents.

The six operation schemas match PayPal's specification. All nineteen tested safeguard mutations are caught. These are offline measurements, not PayPal sandbox acceptance. Anyone can repeat the offline demo.
It is open source, under the MIT licence, and it runs offline in one command, with no PayPal account.
